title: Uber
summary: Ride matching in real time: drivers stream locations into a cell-based geo index, the dispatcher searches neighbouring cells by ETA, and trips run as a strongly consistent state machine.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Rider requests a ride; sees fare estimate and nearby cars
Match the rider to a nearby available driver; driver accepts or declines
Live location tracking during the trip; payment at the end
Match within a few seconds; location updates every ~4 s
A driver is never assigned to two trips (strong consistency on assignment)
Survive a data center failure mid-trip

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: The write-heavy part is location: over a million updates a second, but each one only needs to live a few seconds in memory. Ride requests are small; the hard part is matching correctly and fast.

POST /v1/drivers/location   { lat, lng, heading, ts }          (every 4 s, or over a socket)
POST /v1/rides              { pickup, dropoff, product }     -> { rideId, status: MATCHING }
POST /v1/rides/{id}/accept   (driver)                        -> 200 | 409 already taken
WS   ride updates: DRIVER_ASSIGNED, ARRIVING, IN_TRIP, COMPLETED

head: Data
Key
Store
rows: H3 cell → set of driver_ids; driver_id → (lat, lng, ts, status)
In-memory sharded by cell (Redis / custom ring)
Strongly consistent DB (sharded SQL / Schemaless / Spanner-like)

blocks.caption: Location ingest feeds the geo index; dispatch queries it and assigns atomically

items: Driver app streams location → ingest updates the driver's cell in the geo index and publishes to Kafka.
Rider requests → dispatch computes the pickup cell, reads drivers in that cell and k-ring neighbours, filters available ones.
Rank by road ETA (not straight-line distance), offer to the best driver with a 10–15 s timeout.
On accept, trip service does a conditional update: driver status AVAILABLE → ON_TRIP and trip MATCHING → ASSIGNED, atomically.

head: Option
Fit
rows: Simple; rectangular cells distort; neighbours need 8 lookups
Adapts to density; rebuild cost with constantly moving points
Equal-distance neighbours, hierarchical resolutions, good for surge zones and k-ring search

items: Use a resolution where a cell is ~0.1–1 km²; search ring k=1, expand to k=2..3 if too few drivers.
Shard the index by cell (consistent hashing over cell IDs). A moving driver occasionally changes shard: remove from old cell, add to new.
Locations older than ~30 s are treated as stale and ignored.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd index drivers by H3 cell in memory. Matching is 'read my cell plus neighbours, filter by availability, rank by ETA', so every query touches a handful of keys.

sections.title: Deep dive: matching and avoiding double assignment

items: Greedy nearest-driver is simple; batched matching (collect requests for ~2 s, solve assignment) gives better global ETAs.
Each offer reserves the driver with a short lease (`SET driver:42:offer ride:9 NX PX 15000`) so two dispatchers don't offer the same driver.
Final assignment is a compare-and-set in the trip DB; if it fails (409), dispatch moves to the next candidate.
Trip lifecycle is an explicit state machine: REQUESTED → MATCHING → ASSIGNED → ARRIVED → IN_TRIP → COMPLETED / CANCELLED; every transition idempotent with a version.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Using only the cache to mark a driver busy is unsafe. The lease prevents concurrent offers; the database CAS is the source of truth.

head: Failure
Impact
Mitigation
rows: No drivers visible in an area
Replicas; drivers repopulate within one 4 s update cycle
Trip DB replicated across regions; driver app caches trip state and replays it (Uber used the phone as a backup)
Surge pricing, request queueing, batched matching
Complete trip, charge async with retries and idempotency key

head: Decision
Chose
Gave up
rows: ~1–2 s extra wait for better global ETA

items.title: Non-functional
items.text: Seconds to match, no double booking.

items.title: HLD
items.text: Ingest → geo index; dispatch → trip service CAS.

items.title: Deep dives
items.text: H3 index, matching + leases, trip state machine.

items.title: Wrap-up
items.text: DC failover, surge, monitoring match time and ETA error.

items.q: How do you compute surge pricing?
items.a: Per H3 cell, every ~minute: demand (requests) vs supply (available drivers), smoothed, capped; published to a cache read by pricing.

items.q: How do you show cars moving smoothly on the rider map?
items.a: Client interpolates between 4 s updates using heading and speed; server sends only the assigned driver's updates during the trip.

items.q: Why not store locations in Postgres with PostGIS?
items.a: 1.25M updates/s of short-lived data would overwhelm a relational DB; in-memory cells fit the access pattern.
Road graph with live traffic, precomputed contraction hierarchies, ML correction; cached per cell pair.

items: Locations: 1M+/s, in memory, keyed by H3 cell.
Search = my cell + k-ring neighbours, rank by ETA.
Offer lease prevents double offers; DB CAS prevents double assignment.
Surge per cell from supply vs demand.
